intro: Printing press operators check quality, monitor machines and fix problems fast, skills that many manufacturing jobs need. The closest of the 25 careers below is adhesive bonding machine operation, with an 88% skill match, while gas compressor and pumping station operators earn a BLS May 2025 median of $77,320, which is 69% more.
why_it_works: A press run means setting up plates, adjusting ink and paper and spotting defects before thousands of copies go out. O*NET rates quality control analysis at 3.88 out of 5 for this job and operations monitoring at 3.62. Paper, metal and plastics machine work use the same skills. All 25 matches need no extra schooling. The gaps are installation and programming machines.
tips: Gas plant and pipeline operators earn far more and value your monitoring discipline.
Paper goods machine operators earn $50,270, which is 10% more, in a closely related plant.
Learn basic machine programming; CNC and automated presses pay more than manual ones.

faq.q: What jobs can former printing press operators do?
faq.a: The closest matches are adhesive bonding machine operators (88%), paper goods machine operators (86%) and metal and plastic press machine operators (84%), based on O*NET 31.0. Rolling machine operators are also 84% matched and earn $50,140, which is 10% more than the $45,780 press operator median.

faq.q: Which careers for printing press operators pay more?
faq.a: 16 of the 25 matches pay more. Gas compressor and pumping station operators earn $77,320 (69% more), Engine and Other Machine Assemblers $53,710 (17% more) and milling and planing machine operators $52,800 (15% more), according to BLS May 2025 data.

faq.q: Do printing press operators need more education to switch?
faq.a: No. All 25 matches need no more education than printing press operators already have, including all of the top 10. In the closest match, 73% of workers have a high school diploma or the equivalent, and most training happens on the job.

faq.q: What skills should printing press operators learn?
faq.a: The skills that most often need work are installation, operation and control, operations analysis and programming. Judgment already rates 3.12 out of 5 for this job in O*NET, so learning automated equipment is the main step toward better-paid plant work.
